I'm a pretty big disc collector, and dare I say that we are actually, quietly in a golden age for physical media?

Many classic, foreign and cult films are getting loving high-definition restorations from outfits like Criterion, Severin, Kino Lorber, Vinegar Syndrome, Deaf Crocodile, and many more. 

If you ever loved some crusty old VHS from your local video store, you can probably find a new version on disc featuring pristine visuals, audio and new interviews with cast, crew and film scholars. And, for those who care about such things, you might get appealing new cover art, informative booklets or clever curation in the form of themed boxsets (like Severin's folk horror series). 

No fees. No ad interruptions. No risk of a title suddenly becoming unavailable. 

If there's a tradeoff, it's that despite all the new discs coming to market, the number of companies making 4K UDH blu-ray players is shrinking rapidly. That's sort of a niche concern, though, as there are many standard blu-ray and DVD players on the market.

This vanity war has inflicted heavy collateral damage on the U.S. and global economies. By destabilizing global energy channels, Trump choked baseline petroleum flows down from pre-war highs of roughly 600 million barrels a month (about 20 million barrels per day) to a crippled wartime trickle averaging roughly 300 million to 375 million barrels a month (about 10 to 13 million barrels per day), representing a devastating 37.5% to 50% drop in monthly volume.

This severe supply contraction has sent shockwaves through international shipping, manufacturing, and supply chains, with Moody’s estimating the crisis has cost the average American household nearly $2,000 in lost purchasing power. 

Rather than accepting accountability for a self-inflicted economic wound that is bleeding working-class households dry, the administration gaslights voters while families shoulder billions in extra energy costs.

Equally as vexing is the level of cruelty demonstrated by Blackburn, who has aligned with some pretty awful characters in Washington who should be serving life sentences in federal prison. Instead, they are running the government. 

Ms. Pike should not be given a free pass in the wake of the crime she and her classmates committed all those years ago. But giving her the electric chair after the state committed such a grievous blunder is beyond the scope of normalcy. The woman did the crime, the case was adjudicated, she was sentenced, the state blew it, and now she should be allowed to live her life behind bars. No winners here — just a panoply of pain that is wrenching to everyone involved.

He rails against any notion that things are the way they are because of tradition, or essential ideas, or nature. He believes that societies construct themselves bit by bit over time and that they can reconstruct and reconfigure just as well. The essential element is that individuals must become autonomous and reject the received wisdom of the crowd and must work with other autonomous individuals to construct societies that enhance human freedom, potential and well-being. We should never let anyone speak for us, especially politicians. In doing so we give up our autonomy. Any urge to dominate or exclude must be resisted. Radical democracy is not the domination of a majority, it is a weighing of all voices. It should be like a wave or a rising tide rather than a light switch.

To finance it they suppose that our economy grows by at least 2% annually. To be clear, EACH AND EVERY YEAR. Obviously, our economy doesn't do that. No more than any other. And for many years governments have extended it to ever more people while studiously ignoring the untenability of the system, to the point of borrowing on the financial markets to cover running expenditure. So now, when the conclusion has become undeniable and hard measures must be taken, the voters feel betrayed. And some of them turn to the extremes. comments.body: I agree! I spent 2 weeks in Romania in September 2023 and visited Bran and Peles castles, along with several of the cities mentioned in this article. I feel the author does the readers a disservice in implying they should skip Bran castle. Though Bran (the town) is touristy, I found both castles equally stunning with different and interesting histories. Notably, Bran castle has a light, summary bohemian feel, with its white washed walls - similar to a Mykonos feel, as I recall its last inhabitant, a princess, was an interior designer. It was stunning. Very different from Peles. The discussion of how the royal family was so adored for their love of sharing the arts and music with their subjects, that after the fall of Communism many of their royal residences  were returned to their descendants by the people, and those descendants are in turn helping to restore them through a foundation (or foundations…don’t quote me) was heartwarming. Both castles have their own beauty and should NOT be missed. Most importantly, for anyone who was a fan of Dracula or vampire lore as a kid (or adult) little can beat the remarkable thrill of approaching the imposing Bran Castle up the hill from town and walking up to its gigantic scary doors, about to enter! Once you do, all the horror fades away to a place of great beauty. I highly recommend not missing!

comments.body: We visit Romania from time to time and we always try to spend a week in Transylvania, which is gorgeous. We visited most of the places mentioned in this article (Sighisoara, Brasov, Bran Castle, Peles, Biertan, etc.). This summer we went to Sibiu, an absolutely amazing city. The entire area around it is incredibly beautiful: castles, fortified churches, viaducts, hiking trails, stunning vistas, it's truly a paradise. What's best is that you're in an area where people are friendly and hospitable. And there are so many things to see. The Astra Museum just outside Sibiu, an open air museum of village houses and crafts from all over Romania, was amazing. We also drove to Sarmizegetusa Regia, the ruins of the ancient Dacian capital of Sarmizegetusa, sacked by the Romans in 105-106 CE. Parts of it are still an archeological dig, but the area you can visit looks a lot like Stonehenge. Toward the end of the trip, we drove on the spectacular Transfagarasan mountain road which crosses the Southern Carpathians. An unforgettable experience. I highly recommend Romania, and Transylvania in particular, as a vacation destination.

I regularly listen to fiction books at around 2x speed (typically 2.2 on Kindle text-to-speech, faster for human narrators), and sometimes also watch videos at that speed.  However, when I am watching/listening to something for work (I teach law classes to undergraduates) or to learn something, I need to slow way down, even when it's a familiar topic.  

Maybe other people can process fully at that speed, but for me, more complex concepts require more thought to get from short-term, "entertainment"-level recall to longer-term, understanding-level recall.  I also find that my mind is more likely to wander when I'm not as highly entertained, meaning that the stuff I most want to speed through actually is least amenable to speeding up (if I care about actually learning it).

If I'm previewing or reviewing something that I'll also actually read with my eyes, I need to go down to about 1.5x; for something that I'll ONLY listen to/watch I typically need to get down to 1.2x.  And when I'm trying to learn to DO something new—say, a new cooking or craft technique—I may need to go down to .5x for particularly complicated steps, and rewind them a couple of times.

While I didn't get to see the ballet "Petal," the critic's portrait of it ("pretty moments" but largely unremarkable) suits the Farrar piece perfectly. I, too, thought of "In the Night," but the Farrar piece resembles the Robbins only superficially. 

As for “The Dream," it was good to hear the Young People’s Chorus and that gorgeous score, but the lead couple didn't seem to fully understand their characters.  I found myself wondering if the women had banged their shoes; the fairies were extremely noisy. As a dancer I could ignore the noise, but it sure didn’t contribute to the atmosphere Ashton or Mendelssohn undoubtedly intended to create. A new balletgoer, the type of person I imagine ABT hopes to attract, might wonder why the fairies sounded so clunky. 

It's important for any artist - dancer, young choreographer, or artistic director - to hear the truth about their work. Those criticisms may be harsh, but after all, isn't it true that the most important elements in ballet are an unforced musicality and that rare ability some dancers have to both reveal their innermost selves and illuminate the human condition?

Some random thoughts.  

I have heard of some stately manor house in Britain.  Which went on the market.  But the owners were at pains NOT to inform any prospective buyers--

--that one wing of the house was haunted.  Just as in that old movie classic "The Ghost and Mrs. Muir"--

--those unlucky occupants  would find out soon enough--  

--they were not the sole occupants.  

But some years ago, my wife and I bought our house from a  young couple.  Nice people.  Who left us a bottle of red wine when we moved in.  

But the man had been obliged to spend a night in a club house.  Formerly part of a golf club that'd been turned into a set of town houses.  

And both he and his wife (otherwise normal, right thinking Americans) were utterly convinced:  that club house was haunted.  They had not a particle of doubt.  

But on the other hand--

--does anyone feel sorry for the ghosts? 

Endlessly roaming around their old haunts (no pun intended).  Playing with the furniture. Knocking over bits of crockery.  Scaring people--

--as if that were any fun.  

The lines of Pope come to mind.  Describing elderly ladies at a ball.  

        "As hags hold sabbath less for joy than spite,
         So these their merry miserable night.
         Still round and round the ghosts of beauty glide
         And haunt the places where their honor died."  

Which (in my view) says it all.

Thanks, Ms. Bahr.

comments.body: The "game" here driven by the cabal of realtors, businesses, the descendants of the original wealthy residents, and politicians in Hunterdon County, New Jersey, is to "increase," not decrease the required lot size for homes. Shamelessly, the Director of the Hunterdon County Freeholders bragged in one of the local newspapers not long ago that setting aside space for environmental reasons was nothing but a ploy to keep out affordable housing.He's a charming and typical character among the rich in this most Republican of counties. Apparently his avarice has earned him a recent appointment as a Superior Court Judge in this State. He's the scion of a family of lawyers, so what would he know about living in fear of being of homeless? Not too long ago he was picked up for driving while impaired. Were he a minority he never would have gotten away with refusing the Flemington Borough Police Officer's order that he take a breathalyzer.But it didn't stop there: he insisted his erratic driving was due to his "medication" and demanded to be taken to the Hunterdon Medical Center. No one not among the rich, white, and powerful in this red as a ruby place would have beaten a drunk driving charge. Shame on Governor Mikie Sherrill for appointing a person so heartless about the plight of those who face inexcusable barriers to simply sheltering themselves. Governor Sherrill,a Democrat,  presents herself as the brave former Navy helicopter pilot who stands up to Trump! "Preserved Land" is a ploy.

comments.name: Anonymous
comments.body: I'm writing from the 11th richest County in the USA, Hunterdon, in New Jersey.This is Flemington,the Seat of that County,and what is built here has always been driven by who gets rich in the construction of the project.The nation's largest outdoor outlet center here,Liberty Village and Turntable Junction, now lies in rubble.It probably will be turned into some kind of housing with a bone thrown to some units meeting the definition of "affordable."My father-in-law told officials in Hunterdon County over half a century ago that the building of the outlet center shouldn't be done." The infrastructure can't support it,"he said He had a summer house here, his main residence being in Manhattan where he was Director of Field Services for the Landmarks Preservation Commission. But then as now,the politicians and developers of Hunterdon County made choices based on their own financial interests,not the good of the community.The dirty little secret of Flemington is that the family that reaped the greatest award of building that outlet center made bricks here.When the outlet center was constructed,every inch of the surface of it was brick;the family became multi-millionaires overnight.People in this rural-suburban sprawl of Hunterdon County love to point to the crime and corruption of New York City while destroying here whatever they choose to enrich themselves,the freeholders,and the entrenched wealthy.That rapacious brick making family has some descendants left--all multimillionaires.

comments.body: Thanks for this cool story, giving us a peek into the house and its thoughtful owners! It's been a kind of Houdiniesque week for me. You see, on Wednesday, by sheer coincidence, I spent time online in the morning looking at awesome pictures of Art Deco skyscrapers in Detroit, built around the time Houdini died there. Then later I watched a webinar about a new book called Houdini's Library, detailing his fantastic collection of magic and theatrical memorabilia. I got a copy and have been perusing this book since, filled with images of his treasures and the photos he also took in his international travels of collecting and meeting his own idols of magic, with whom he often took keepsake photos. And now a friend in Chicago just happened to alert me to this lovely article, when I called to wish her a Happy Birthday today on Halloween. So I feel the presence of this amazing man today, on the centenary of his tragic passing. But no ordinary celebrity he, for Houdini somehow feels immortal!

comments.body: I couldn't get past the copy editing (really the lack of it) in this book.  Last name Lefleur?  In French it's Lafleur.  The word for "flower" is feminine. Are we not supposed to notice?  "Welp?"  In 1933?  Come on.  Endless use of "alright," except once, when it is rendered as "all right."  The song Meg hears on the radio is not "Ten Cents for a Dance."  It's "Ten Cents a Dance" (by Rodgers and Hart).  I'm all for using pop magazines for period research, but not at the expense of some archival (and plain old grammatical) stuff, too.  The errors may yield "relatability," but for this reader they resulted in my not trusting the author.  And/or the publisher.  Anyone want to take on the Jack London connection?

comments.name: Jane Roberts
comments.body:
I loved this story. The author is a wonderful storyteller and the characters are delightfully interesting and often funny. I grew up in the South, and saw many folks I knew in this book. 

There are many plots going on, but I loved the characters the most. Birdie was my favorite, a misfit who makes the best of her life. But all the “ladies” were quite interesting. Their various life stories gave the reader an understanding of who each really was. Meg was quite a hoot! She was put in impossible situations, but handled them with humor and ingenuity. Smart girl!  My impression of most of the female characters, except Frances of course, was of strong women who did what had to be done to survive. Even Garnett, who was truly evil and most unlikeable, was a strong woman. 

The ending was rather sad for me. While many wrongs were make right at the end, I wanted to learn what happens to the characters next.

comments.name: Evelyn Nunez
comments.body: Getting through a challenging time period in my life took a very long time and honestly it's still something I'm coping through. Grief is a feeling everyone recognizes whether it was a family loss, pet loss, friendship breakup, and more. In my case, I was grieving over the loss of someone who's still alive but just isn't present in my life. It was difficult trying to get past the fact that someone who was supposed to be a role model turned out to be the person I would never want to become or seem like. Emotions like anger, denial, hurt, and sadness were all feelings that I constantly battled with and it was hard for my younger self to have to endure those feelings on my own while also trying to help others going through the same thing. The biggest help for me was going to therapy and speaking with a professional who knew how to guide me through my grief and the proper coping  mechanisms. Although I did have family and some friends to sort of comfort me, it wasn't something I relied on because it was more of me reaching out instead of the other way around so I found peace in my solitude.
